messages.author: 40e173783f466ae0
messages.subject: n.eff from jagsUI
parts: Is there a good source explaining what the n.eff produced in the output from jagsUI is? I'm under the impression it's related to how well the estimates from the posterior are and that you generally want it to be in the 1,000's.

messages.author: ecb9dc91d7ca3aa8
messages.subject: Re: n.eff from jagsUI
parts:
Tim,

My guess would be (without looking into jagsUI) is that it is effective sample size as reported by Partyn Plummer's {coda} package (it also appears in mcmc.list object summaries), see http://ugrad.stat.ubc.ca/R/library/coda/html/effectiveSize.html

The idea is to correct for non-independence due to autocorrelation in the MCMC chains (especially when thin=1).

Cheers,

Peter

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: n.eff from jagsUI
parts:
The idea that a correction is needed to account for non-independence is introduced on p. 8 of the Handbook of MCMC, with estimation methods appearing on p.13.  An early informal discussion including the term "effective sample size" is Kass et al. 1998.

One might argue that effective sample size (ESS, or n.eff) is such a fundamental quantity to MCMC that it is not just a metric to check but one of the most basic features of a chain.  It answers perhaps the most basic question of an MCMC sample: how accurate is the estimate of the posterior mean?  If n samples X_i are independent, then

Var[ Mean[X_i] ]  = Var[X_i] / n

Since MCMC samples are sequentially dependent, we have instead that

Var[ Mean[X_i] ] = Var[X_i] / n.eff

In other words, n.eff lets us estimate the standard error of estimates of the mean from an MCMC chain. This is basically what is stated in the coda package's documentation given in Peter's initial answer.  The point is that it is so fundamental that one could argue it doesn't need citation any more than a standard error needs citation.

One might instead give a citation for estimation methods for ESS, of which there are many.  It should be noted that when a chain mixes really poorly, the estimates of ESS will not be very accurate.  The method in package coda, which I'm guessing might be used by jagsUI based on its Imports list, tends to over-estimate n.eff for very slowly mixing chains.  This occurs because it relies on fitting an auto-regressive time-series model to the chain, with a maximum order set by default behavior of the ar() function, which can be too small for very slow mixing.  Other packages like mcmcse provide other methods.

-Perry
